title: First words
goal: Greet people politely, say yes and no, thank, apologise and take your leave in Telugu.
intro:
Telugu greetings are warm and a little formal. The all-purpose greeting is *నమస్కారం* (namaskāram), said with palms joined. Politeness is carried by the little word *అండి* (aṇḍi), which you can add to almost anything to make it respectful: *సరే అండి* (okay, sir/madam).

Telugu also has a charming way of saying goodbye: you don't say 'I'm going', you say *వెళ్ళొస్తాను* (veḷḷostānu), 'I'll go and come back'.

vocab.note: Also used for goodbye in formal settings.

vocab.en: sure, will do; in that way

vocab.note: In speech, థాంక్స్ (thāṅks) is far more common.
Often replaced by a polite verb ending -aṇḍi.
Attach to words: అవునండి avunaṇḍi, yes (polite).
Comes after the word: నేను కూడా, me too.
Used in media; people usually just say నమస్కారం.

phrases.en: Go and come back (reply to goodbye).

grammar.title: Word order: subject–object–verb
grammar.body:
Telugu puts the **verb at the end** of the sentence: *I tea drink*, not *I drink tea*. Question words and objects come before the verb.

Because the verb ending already shows who is acting (*-ānu* = I, *-āru* = you polite / they, *-āḍu* = he), the subject pronoun is often left out: *వస్తాను* (vastānu) alone means 'I'll come'.

grammar.title: Polite and informal 'you': మీరు and నువ్వు
grammar.body:
Telugu has two words for *you*. **మీరు** (mīru) is polite (and also plural): use it with strangers, elders, anyone you would call 'sir' or 'madam'. **నువ్వు** (nuvvu) is intimate: for close friends, younger siblings, children.

The verb agrees: *మీరు ఉన్నారు* (mīru unnāru) but *నువ్వు ఉన్నావు* (nuvvu unnāvu). Commands also have two forms: polite **-aṇḍi** (*రండి* raṇḍi, come) vs informal bare stem (*రా* rā, come).

To be extra polite, add **అండి** (aṇḍi) to a word or sentence: *అవునండి* (yes, sir/madam), *థాంక్స్ అండి*. When in doubt, use మీరు and -aṇḍi.

dialogue.title: Meeting a neighbour
dialogue.setting: Lakshmi runs into her older neighbour, Mr Rao, at his gate in the morning.

lines.speaker: Rao
lines.en: I'm fine too. Come in, have a seat.

lines.speaker: Lakshmi
lines.native: థాంక్స్ అండి. కానీ ఇప్పుడు టైం లేదు.
lines.roman: thāṅks aṇḍi. kānī ippuḍu ṭaim lēdu.
lines.en: Thank you. But I don't have time now.

lines.speaker: Rao
lines.en: Fine, go well (go and come back).

culture: Saying 'I'm going' (వెళ్తాను) when leaving sounds blunt, even ominous, to many Telugu speakers; *వెళ్ళొస్తాను* ('I'll go and come') and the reply *వెళ్ళి రండి* ('go and come') are the polite way to part. English 'thanks', 'sorry' and 'okay' are completely normal in everyday speech, while *ధన్యవాదాలు* sounds formal, as on TV or at a function. Between family members, explicit thanks can even sound distant.
